\begin{abstract}
Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation can answer a document question from optical character
recognition (OCR) text, a retrieved page image, or both, at different GPU cost. Serving it at scale is
a GPU provisioning problem: generation compute grows with the request rate, and an uncompressed late-interaction
visual index grows with the corpus, to 246\,GiB at a million pages. We present the Cost-Aware Visual
Router (CAVR), which chooses the answer path per query under a cost weight set per deployment. On one
RTX 4090, we run every path on 8,150 DocVQA and InfographicVQA questions with one shared generator, measuring
average normalised Levenshtein similarity (ANLS), GPU-seconds, energy and latency. Against the strongest fixed
policy, the page image alone, the content-aware variant CAVR-CE, a cross-encoder (CE) over the retrieved passages,
gains 0.016 ANLS for 15\% more GPU compute; against always using both contexts, it saves 29\% at
0.008 lower ANLS. In simulation, 100 queries/s at a p95 latency of
2\,s needs 72 GPUs with CAVR-CE, 106 with both contexts and
64 with the page image alone; served live with vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs, the policies kept
this order at a p95 of 5\,s but reached 1.4--2.0$\times$ less capacity than simulated. On
1,499 held-out questions from the datasets' training splits, which ColPali and possibly the generator saw in
training, CAVR-CE kept a 35\% saving over both contexts but was 0.005 ANLS above the page
image alone (not significant). Our earlier keyword-rule labels agree with measured outcomes no better than chance.
\end{abstract}
